passage:
Sunday night
Dear Diary,
Science project is due tomorrow. On Friday I told Mumma it would take ten minutes, just a volcano with baking soda. Easy!
But first I couldn't find the clay. Then Nazia didi was using the glue. Then my volcano fell over twice because the bottle was too tall. It's ten o'clock now and it's still wet and brown and sad.
Mumma said, "My boy and his ten minutes." She reminded me that with the solar system model I also said ten minutes, and we were up till eleven. I forgot all about that. Every time, I think it will be quick. Next time I'm starting on Friday. Maybe.
Tavish

qa.q: What kept making Tavish's volcano fall over?
qa.a: It fell over twice because the bottle was too tall.

qa.q: Why did Tavish think the project would take ten minutes?
qa.a: Tavish felt confident because he pictured only the easy volcano and forgot the solar system model, when he also said ten minutes and was up till eleven.

qa.q: What could Tavish try for the next project?
qa.a: He could remember how long the last one took, gather the clay and glue early, and really start on Friday.

qa.q: What is Sunday night like for Mumma?
qa.a: Mumma is up late with a wet volcano she saw coming, since the same thing happened with the solar system model.

grounding: A boy expects his volcano project to take ten minutes and starts the night before, forgetting his last project ran late.

passage: In Kainakary, where every house faces the canal, Thomas had two weeks to make a leaf album for his EVS class: twenty different leaves, pressed and labelled. "Easy. One evening," he told his friend Noor as they fished off the jetty. Every evening after that there was cricket, or fishing, or the ferry to watch. On the last night Thomas ran around the compound with a torch, pulling leaves off the jackfruit and banana trees. The coconut leaf was too big to press. The hibiscus leaves curled in the heat of the lamp. Half the names he didn't know. At eleven, Ammachi found him asleep on the verandah beside twelve crumpled leaves. It was exactly what had happened with his shell collection last term, though he hadn't thought of it once.

qa.q: How many leaves did the album need?
qa.a: Twenty different leaves, pressed and labelled.

qa.q: Why did Thomas say it would take one evening?
qa.a: Thomas felt confident because he pictured the smooth version of the task and never thought of his shell collection last term, so it felt easy.

qa.q: What small step could have helped Thomas in the first week?
qa.a: He could have collected a few leaves each evening before fishing or cricket, so the last night wasn't a scramble.

qa.q: How might Ammachi feel finding Thomas asleep on the verandah?
qa.a: Ammachi may feel tender and a bit worried, seeing him worn out beside only twelve crumpled leaves.

grounding: A boy thinks a two-week leaf album will take one evening and scrambles the night before, having forgotten a similar delay.

passage: On Sunday evening in their Berlin apartment block, Pablo knocked on Zeynep's door. "Can I borrow your coloured pencils? My castle poster is due tomorrow." Zeynep's eyes went wide. "You said it would take half an hour. That was three weeks ago." "It will take half an hour," Pablo said. "Draw the castle, write three facts, done." Back home, he spent forty minutes on the drawbridge alone. Then he couldn't find the book with the castle facts. Then his little brother spilled juice on one corner. At ten, his father found him close to tears with only the towers finished. "Remember the dinosaur poster?" his father said softly. Pablo did, now. That one was going to take half an hour too.

qa.q: What did Pablo ask to borrow from Zeynep?
qa.a: He asked to borrow her coloured pencils.

qa.q: Why was Pablo sure the poster would take half an hour?
qa.a: Pablo felt confident because he imagined only 'draw the castle, write three facts, done', and didn't think of the dinosaur poster that had also run late. 😔

qa.q: What would you advise Pablo for his next poster?
qa.a: Think back to how long the dinosaur poster really took, start weeks earlier, and do one part at a time.

qa.q: How might Zeynep see Pablo's plan?
qa.a: Zeynep remembers his 'half an hour' from three weeks ago, so she can see the trouble coming more clearly than he can.

grounding: A boy believes a poster will take half an hour, starts the night before, and only then remembers a similar project.

passage:
Study hour at the boys' hostel began at seven. Vijay, ten, had a clay model of the water cycle due the next morning. "Ten minutes," he told Preeti didi, the evening warden. "Clay, cloud, arrow, done."
"Last month your map took two evenings," she reminded him.
"That was different. This one is easy."
At 7:30 he found the clay was hard and had to soak it. At 8:00 his cloud kept falling off the cardboard. At 8:40 he realised he hadn't written the labels. The lights-out bell rang at nine, and the arrows were still missing. Vijay stared at his sticky fingers, eyes shiny.
Preeti didi sat down beside him. "Tell me, how long did the map really take?" she asked.
"Two evenings," he mumbled.

qa.q: At what time did the lights-out bell ring?
qa.a: The lights-out bell rang at nine.

qa.q: Why did Vijay feel so sure the model would take only ten minutes?
qa.a: He felt confident, picturing it going perfectly, clay, cloud, arrow, done, so he forgot how long his map had taken last month.

qa.q: What could Vijay try next time a project is due?
qa.a: He could remember how long the map really took and start a few days earlier, breaking the model into small jobs like soaking the clay and writing labels.

qa.q: How might Preeti didi feel sitting beside Vijay at the end?
qa.a: She probably feels sorry for him with his sticky fingers and shiny eyes, and hopes her gentle question helps him remember the map next time.

grounding: It shows a boy promising a project will be quick, starting the night before and forgetting how long his last project took.

passage:
I'm Damini, and I live across the landing from Tanvir's family. He's nine. On Sunday afternoon he knocked on our door holding a shoebox. "Damini didi, can I borrow glue? My solar system project is due tomorrow. It'll only take a bit."
He'd had two weeks. I remembered his mother saying his volcano last term had taken the whole weekend, with tears.
At six, he came back for scissors. At eight, for black paper. At nine thirty I heard him through the wall saying, "Why won't Saturn stay up?" and his mother sighing.
The next morning, on the stairs, he looked tired but proud, holding a shoebox with eight wobbly planets. I don't know what he was thinking all those hours. But when I asked how long it took, he said, "Just a bit," and then, after a second, "Actually, a lot."

qa.q: What was Tanvir's project about?
qa.a: It was a solar system project in a shoebox.

qa.q: What does Tanvir saying 'It'll only take a bit' suggest about how he imagined the project?
qa.a: It suggests he felt confident and relaxed, picturing it going smoothly with no problems, and did not remember how long his volcano had taken last term.

qa.q: What small step could help Tanvir next time he has a two-week project?
qa.a: He could start on the first weekend and do one part at a time, like painting planets one day and sticking them the next, since he now knows it takes a lot.

qa.q: How might Tanvir's mother feel during that Sunday evening?
qa.a: His mother, heard sighing at nine thirty, probably feels tired and a little frustrated, having seen the same last-minute rush with the volcano.

grounding: Told by a neighbour, it shows a boy expecting a project to be quick and starting the night before, forgetting earlier delays.

passage:
"Anand, isn't your solar system model due tomorrow?" asked Bhavna didi, looking up from her phone.
"Yes. It'll take ten minutes. I just need balls and paint."
"Do you have balls and paint?"
"Mummy has... something."
"Last time the volcano took you all Sunday."
"That was a volcano. This is just circles."
"Planets, a sun, sticks, labels..."
"It's easy, didi."
At 8 p.m. Anand was on the floor with newspaper and a half-painted Jupiter. At 9:30 the paint on Saturn still hadn't dried. At 10:15 he was crying because Mars had rolled under the sofa.
Bhavna crouched down beside him with a torch. "Ten minutes, na?" she said, and fished out Mars.

qa.q: What rolled under the sofa?
qa.a: Mars.

qa.q: Why was Anand so sure the model would take ten minutes?
qa.a: He felt confident and pictured only the easy path, forgetting that the volcano took all Sunday, so it seemed quick.

qa.q: What could Anand try for the next project?
qa.a: Remember how long the last one really took, list every part, and start a few days early.

qa.q: How does Bhavna didi seem to feel at 10:15?
qa.a: She seems amused but kind, teasing him gently while fishing out Mars with a torch.

grounding: A boy insists his model will take ten minutes, starts the night before and forgets how long his last project took.

passage: Last month our teacher gave us two weeks to write a book report. I thought, easy, it's only one page, I'll do it on the last night. I told Amandeep I'd finish in half an hour. Amandeep started reading the book on the first day. On the last night I opened the book and saw it had 160 pages. I had forgotten that I read slowly, and that the poem assignment took me three evenings. I read until eleven and only got to page 70. Papa found me asleep on the book. In the morning I wrote half a page about the first half. Now I think my brain shows me the fastest way it could go, not the way it usually goes. Deepak, 160 pages is not half an hour.

qa.q: How many pages did the book have?
qa.a: 160 pages.

qa.q: Why did Deepak think the report would take only half an hour?
qa.a: Deepak felt calm and confident, picturing the quickest way it could go and forgetting past slowness, like the poem that took three evenings.

qa.q: What could Deepak do with the next two-week assignment?
qa.a: Check how big the job is on the first day, remember how long similar work took, and do a little each day like Amandeep.

qa.q: How might Amandeep have felt the morning the report was due?
qa.a: Amandeep was probably relaxed and ready, having started reading on the first day.

grounding: A child recalls planning a book report for the last night, imagining the fastest path and forgetting past delays.

passage:
Class 4 teacher's note, science fair week
On Monday I asked each pair to estimate how long their diorama would take. Sahil said, "One evening, Miss. Easy." His partner Dolma said, "Maybe four evenings," and he laughed at her. When I reminded Sahil that his last project, the paper bridge, had taken him a week and still wasn't finished on the day, he said, "This one's different. It's smaller." The pair started on Thursday night. On Friday morning they arrived with a painted box, no animals and no labels. Sahil looked close to tears. Dolma had made the animals at home anyway, just in case, and they finished at lunch. I have asked every pair to write down how long their last project actually took before planning the next one.

qa.q: What did Dolma estimate?
qa.a: Maybe four evenings.

qa.q: Why did Sahil laugh at Dolma's estimate?
qa.a: He felt confident and sure it would be easy, imagining the quick version and ignoring how the paper bridge took a week.

qa.q: Why is the teacher's new step helpful?
qa.a: Writing down how long the last project actually took makes children plan from real experience instead of the best-case picture.

qa.q: What might Dolma have felt on Friday morning?
qa.a: Dolma was probably relieved and a bit proud that her just-in-case animals saved the project.

grounding: A teacher records a boy who was sure a project would take one evening, ignoring his past delays, and ran out of time.

passage:
Monday.
Miss gave us the solar system model project, due Friday. Dilnaz from next door started hers the same evening. I told her mine would take ten minutes, because I'm Pranav, the fastest boy in class. I'll do it Thursday night.
Thursday night.
It is 10:30 and I am still painting Saturn. The thermocol balls took forever to cut. The paint won't dry. Jupiter fell off the stick twice. Ammi is helping with the hair dryer and she is not happy. I forgot that last time, the volcano project, I also started late and cried at midnight.
Friday.
It was finished at 6 a.m. Saturn's rings are sticky. Dilnaz's model had moons.

qa.q: How many times did Jupiter fall off the stick?
qa.a: Jupiter fell off the stick twice.

qa.q: What was Pranav feeling on Thursday night at 10:30?
qa.a: He felt stressed and a bit panicky, still painting Saturn long after he thought he'd be done.

qa.q: What could Pranav do for the next project?
qa.a: He could remember how long the volcano project really took and start the same evening, like Dilnaz, instead of planning for ten minutes.

qa.q: How might Ammi feel helping with the hair dryer late at night?
qa.a: Ammi is probably tired and annoyed, because the late start turned into her problem too.

grounding: A child's diary shows him expecting a project to take ten minutes, starting the night before and forgetting his past delays.

passage: In Ghoti village, Class 5 had to make a leaf book: twenty different leaves, pressed and labelled. It was due on Monday. "It'll take me ten minutes," Vijay told his sister Tanuja on Friday. "The leaves are right there, on the trees." Tanuja reminded him of the seed chart he'd rushed last term. "That was different," Vijay said. On Sunday afternoon he went out to collect. Some leaves were too high. The tamarind leaves were too small to label. The neem ones curled up in the heat. By sunset he had eleven. He went to bed with the book half empty, his stomach in a knot. Tanuja slipped a torch under his pillow in case he wanted to try the mango tree at dawn.

qa.q: How many leaves did Vijay have by sunset on Sunday?
qa.a: By sunset he had eleven.

qa.q: What was Vijay feeling when he went to bed on Sunday?
qa.a: He felt anxious, his stomach in a knot, because the leaf book was only half done after he'd expected ten minutes.

qa.q: What would you advise Vijay for his next project?
qa.a: Remember how long the seed chart really took and start on the day the project is given, not the day before it is due.

qa.q: How does Tanuja see Vijay's plan?
qa.a: Tanuja remembers his rushed seed chart, so she seems doubtful but kind, helping with a torch for dawn.

grounding: Shows a village child expecting a leaf project to take ten minutes, forgetting past rushes and running short of time.

passage: Emil had a poster on volcanoes due Wednesday at his school in Stockholm. On Monday, Soo-ah asked if he wanted to work in the library after class. "No need," Emil said. "It's one poster. Ten minutes." He pictured it: print three photos, write a title, done. On Tuesday evening he sat down at the kitchen table. The printer was out of ink. His mother drove him to the shop in the snow. The facts he'd found didn't fit on the paper, so he rewrote them twice. At nine his father found him in tears over a glue stick that had dried out. Emil remembered, too late, the same thing had happened with the Viking poster in autumn. Soo-ah's poster, finished on Monday, had a paper volcano that popped out.

qa.q: What was the printer out of on Tuesday evening?
qa.a: The printer was out of ink.

qa.q: What was Emil feeling at nine o'clock?
qa.a: He was upset and overwhelmed, in tears over a dried-out glue stick after expecting the poster to take ten minutes.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could fix it next time?
qa.a: Emil pictured only the ideal path and forgot the Viking poster; next time he could plan for things going wrong and start on Monday like Soo-ah.

qa.q: How might Emil's parents feel about Tuesday evening?
qa.a: They were probably tired and a little frustrated, with a drive in the snow and a crying child late at night.

grounding: Shows a child imagining a poster will take ten minutes, starting the night before and forgetting a similar delay in the past.

passage:
It was the last week before the Christmas break at the boarding school, and the science models were due Monday. On Sunday evening, in the hostel study hall, Thomas finally opened his box of craft sticks.

"How long will your volcano take?" asked Hrithik, who had finished his solar-system mobile days ago.

"Ten minutes. Maybe twenty."

"Last time, your bridge took two whole evenings."

"That was different. This is easy."

By eight, the papier-mâché was still wet. By nine, the paint wouldn't dry. By lights-out, the volcano had a crack down one side.

Thomas stared at it. "I thought it would be quick."

"You always think that," Hrithik said. "Next time, start when I do."

Thomas nodded. He'd only pictured the volcano finished, not all the drying in between.

qa.q: What was Hrithik's model?
qa.a: His solar-system mobile.

qa.q: Why did Thomas think the volcano would take only ten minutes?
qa.a: Thomas felt confident and hopeful, picturing the finished volcano and forgetting how long the bridge had taken.

qa.q: What could Thomas do before the next project?
qa.a: Thomas could remember how long past models took, like the two-evening bridge, and start several days early.

qa.q: How might Hrithik feel watching Thomas rush?
qa.a: Hrithik probably feels a mix of sympathy and mild frustration, since Hrithik has seen this happen before.

grounding: During the last school week before Christmas, a child thinks a model will take ten minutes and starts the night before.

passage:
First day of the Diwali holidays. Harsha's teacher had set a holiday project: a scrapbook on festivals of India. "Ten minutes a day, easy," Harsha told his sister Sunaina. "I'll do it later."

Fourth day. Sunaina reminded him. "Last summer your holiday project took you the whole last week."

"That was harder. This is just pasting pictures."

Last evening of the holidays. Harsha sat surrounded by old magazines, glue on his fingers, and only three pages done out of ten.

"I thought it would be quick," he said, close to tears.

Sunaina sat down and helped him cut. "You always imagine the easy version," she said.

He finished at midnight, with seven pages instead of ten. Next time, he promised, he'd start on day one.

qa.q: How many pages had Harsha done on the last evening?
qa.a: Only three pages done out of ten.

qa.q: How did Harsha feel on the last evening of the holidays?
qa.a: Harsha felt stressed and close to tears, shocked that the easy project took so long.

qa.q: What could Harsha do differently on the next holiday project?
qa.a: Harsha could remember last summer's delay and start on day one, doing a little each day.

qa.q: How might Sunaina have felt helping him at the last minute?
qa.a: Sunaina probably felt sympathetic but also a bit tired of seeing the same pattern.

grounding: Over the festival holidays, a child thinks a scrapbook will be quick and leaves it to the last night.

passage:
Mridul, you're telling me the kite project will take ten minutes? Hmm. Let your grandfather Joseph tell you about Onam when I was ten.

Our teacher asked us to build a model snake boat for the school display. I told my mother, "It'll take me one evening." I'd made paper boats before.

I waited until the night before. The glue took hours to dry. My mother made me tea at eleven and asked, "Wasn't it supposed to take one evening?"

I cried a bit. I'd pictured only the finished boat, shining, not the slow parts in between.

I took a half-finished boat to school. My friend Anil's was beautiful. He'd started a week earlier.

So, Mridul, how long did your last project really take?

qa.q: What did the teacher ask young Joseph's class to build?
qa.a: A model snake boat for the school display.

qa.q: How did young Joseph feel when the boat wasn't done by the night before?
qa.a: Young Joseph felt upset and cried a bit, having pictured only the shining finished boat.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Joseph's story?
qa.a: Taking a half-finished boat while Anil's was beautiful showed Joseph that starting early matters more than hoping it will be quick.

qa.q: How might young Joseph's mother have felt making tea at eleven?
qa.a: His mother probably felt patient but gently amused, having heard the one-evening promise before.

grounding: An elder recalls thinking as a boy that a school model would take one evening and starting the night before.

passage: On the last night of the winter holidays, Yusuf finally took out the science project sheet: a model of a volcano, due tomorrow. "Ten minutes," he told his brother Tejas. "Just some clay and paint." Tejas raised an eyebrow. "Your solar system took the whole Diwali weekend." "That was different. Planets are round." The stationery shop downstairs had its shutter down for the holiday, so there was no clay. Yusuf mixed flour and water instead. It was sticky and kept sliding off the bottle. Then the power went out. By candlelight, with Ammi holding the torch, the volcano leaned sideways like a sleepy dog. At eleven, Yusuf was still painting and yawning, quite sure that next time it really would take ten minutes.

qa.q: What was Yusuf's science project?
qa.a: A model of a volcano, due tomorrow.

qa.q: Why did Yusuf believe the volcano would take ten minutes?
qa.a: He pictured the easy version, just clay and paint, and felt confident and hopeful, forgetting how long the solar system model had taken.

qa.q: What could Yusuf try with his next project?
qa.a: Remember how long the last model really took, check early what materials he needs, and start several days before it is due.

qa.q: How does Tejas see Yusuf's ten-minute plan?
qa.a: Tejas is doubtful and a bit amused, remembering that the solar system took the whole Diwali weekend.

grounding: Shows a child saying a project will be quick and starting the night before, imagining the ideal path and forgetting past delays.
